newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB profit rises, dollar hides improvement.
newsitem.headline: ABB profit rises, dollar hides improvement.

text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG Thursday reported a smaller-than-expected rise in first-half profits as the strong dollar hid a steady improvement in the electrical engineering group's operating earnings.
"Look at the operating performance and look at the currencies, this is a strong performance," ABB's chief executive Goran Lindahl said.
ABB's group net profit in the first six months of 1997 rose 2 percent to $567 million from last year, below the 4.5 percent rise that had been forecast by industry analysts.
ABB's first-half operating earnings rose 3 percent to $1.09 billion, helped by all business segments, while revenue fell 2.6 percent to $15.2 billion on continued weak demand from Western Europe.
But Lindahl said the results were in line with what ABB had promised financial markets and some analysts had forgotten to take the strength of the dollar into account.

Although ABB is owned by Swedish and Swiss parent companies, the group reports in U.S. dollars. The strength of the dollar against European currencies tends to reduce its group results and inflate the results of its parent companies.
"In light of a better backlog, growing orders and that the business environment does not get worse, then it is encouraging for the future," Lindahl said.
New orders to ABB in the first half rose 14 percent to $20.0 billion -- pushing the order backlog up to $35.3 billion -- on strong growth in large projects and increased demand from emerging markets.
ABB also confirmed its forecast for 1997 net profit to at least reach 1996's $1.23 billion, a forecast that Lindahl has described as setting a minimum for what profits could be.
Analysts on average forecast a 5.0 percent increase in ABB's 1997 net profit to $1.295 billion from 1996's $1.233 billion.
Profits from the United Staes also continued to improve and results from Latin America were substantially higher than last year. Earnings from the Asian-Pacific region were unchanged.
ABB's worldwide workforce grew to 216,000 from 215,000, mainly due to new ventures and acquisitions.
